utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, technicians, interpreters; good morning, our legal assistants, court reporters; good morning, registrar; good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Cayley; good morning, Defence counsel: Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic; good morning, General Krstic. Good morning to our witness. Madam, could you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated now. Could you perhaps come a little closer to the microphone so that we can hear you well. Are you comfortable, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. First of all, you will be answering questions that will be put to you, let me guess, by Mr. Harmon. So first of all, you will be asking questions that will be put to you by Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. Could you please state your name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: My name is Teufik Ibrahimefendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is the year when you were born?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to start with your educational background, and we'll go through your educational background. Could you please start by telling us what your secondary education was, secondary school education?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I completed a secondary medical school in Tuzla in 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Between 1970 and 1972, did you attend a higher school, majoring in sociology?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I completed a higher cycle of education, and I was trained as a social worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Between 1975 and 1980, did you attend the University of Sarajevo and did you ultimately graduate with a degree in psychology and pedagogy?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go through your additional coursework that you have taken. Starting in 1995 and 1996, did you receive a certificate for additional coursework that you took that was sponsored, this course, by the World Health Organisation and Columbia University, and did you study and take coursework related to courses in war trauma?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, I took a very intensive course on war trauma and I obtained certificates from Columbia University, from the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, between 1996 and 1997, did you take coursework sponsored by the University of Koln, and could you describe the course and the programme to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: That programme contained psychosocial counselling for the work with traumatised women and children, and it took about 300 hours of intensive education. It was held in Croatia, in the small town of Tucepi, but it was organised under the auspices under the University of Koln, experts from Koln and a lady who came from Vienna; Sabina Schaeffer and Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, between 1998 and this year, did you take an additional 300 hours of training in psychodrama?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It is called psychodrama. The term refers to a special method of work with women and children, and we were specialised in that particular therapy and trained to work with women and children traumatised by war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The programme that you've just referred to, was that sponsored by the European Community?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At present are you currently pursuing course work in Gestalt therapy?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, since February 2000. Again, it is organised by a university from Germany but it has its seat in Zagreb. They have organised a course which is going to take three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is Gestalt therapy, and how does it relate to your present work?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Gestalt therapy is a special kind of psychotherapeutic method designed for work with people with various kinds of problems. But it proved to be specially effective during the war because its methods and techniques were particularly well-designed and well-appreciated in the field of work with traumatised persons. The main objective of this particular therapy is to emphasise the relationship between the therapist and the client, the patient, which is very important in the field of war trauma because it is necessary to establish confidence and an open dialogue which will hopefully lead to the client -- which will enable us to reach the client, reach the patient, at a very close level. And the idea is for the patient to become as open as possible during that kind of therapy so that he can talk about his or her experience which is of a particular importance for the war trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Ibrahimefendic, in addition to that course work, you've taken various seminars that relate to your present work, including seminars in body therapy in trauma and also expressing one's self through painting. Now, can you describe very briefly that type of coursework and the relevance of that coursework to your present-day work?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Let me say first of all that Tuzla as a town was a very interesting place for experts coming from all over the world because of a large number of refugees who were accommodated in Tuzla. And those experts came to Tuzla to share their knowledge about the war trauma together with us who had vast practical experience in working with war trauma. So during the summer we would cooperate with universities from all over the world, and experts specialised in war trauma would come to Tuzla to work with us, and we would work together on our cases. They assisted us. They supervised us in our work. And one such course was the course in expressing one's self through painting, which helped me a lot in my work with women because traumatised women and children, of course, are having lots of difficulties expressing themselves verbally about their problems and about their feelings, about their pain and their worries. But the idea of expressing one's self through painting was very good and very helpful for us, and it helped us assess the situation they found themselves in. And it was easier for us to assess their problems through their paintings than through conversations that we had with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to your work background. Between 1967 and 1970, did you work as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I worked as a pediatric nurse. I worked with sick children who had been hospitalised for a very long time who were suffering from tuberculosis. And my work involved children who spent a lot of time in hospital and who had problems adjusting themselves to the life in hospital and who also had difficulties relating to their education due to their prolonged hospitalisation which would cause interruption in their education. So that was the kind of work that I did during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, from 1970 until 1994, were you a psychiatric social worker at the clinical centre at the hospital in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And very briefly, could you describe your duties and responsibilities while working in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: My job, my employment, was actually with the blood transfusion department, because at that time the situation in Bosnia was such that a large number of people had to be mobilised and encouraged to give blood. And people needed to be adequately informed, and they had to be made altruistic and made aware of the need to help the wounded and the sick. So that was my task, that was my job. And I worked with a large group of people, large group of the local population involving younger people at lessons up to the adults of the age of 70, for example. And I worked with hospitals, with schools, with public companies. It was a vast network and system of blood donors. We were in charge of looking for people, finding people who would be willing to give blood and providing the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, from 1994 until the present, are you employed at Vive Zene?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday the Judges heard from the director of that programme and a description of that programme, which is a multidisciplinary programme, treating war trauma victims, women, children, both in an in-house situation and in the community itself. You, Mrs. Ibrahimefendic, are the coordinator of the multidisciplinary teams, are you not?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to that responsibility at Vive Zene, you treat the women and the children yourself; you have your own caseload. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, we're going to be using terms throughout the remainder of this morning's testimony, the words "trauma" and the words "war trauma." Could you define for us first the term "trauma" and then the term "war trauma," and distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Trauma refers to an event which cannot be termed as a normal event in an individual's life. It is a kind of emotional shock that can result in harm and damage to the personality of the individual and which can cause substantial changes in the personality of the individual. Trauma was the most -- one of the most common forms of trauma was the war trauma. War trauma is especially significant and important because it involves a large number of people. These are usually -- this usually happens in difficult situations, situations of disasters where an individual's life is threatened and individual's integrity is threatened. Cases that cause war trauma are, for example, the breakup of families and other similar events that threaten an individual's life. The events that took place in Tuzla or elsewhere in Bosnia during the war are various in their scope, and during our work we came to the conclusion that for certain people, the war events were especially hard, such as: the scarcity of food or water; detention; being witness to war events; feeling that you can be killed; feeling that your life is threatened; the very sight of the wounded people; the injured people; to be present during the shelling or bombardment. And people react in different ways to traumatic -- to various traumatic events. And people have -- usually have traumatic reactions when their families are breaking up. A traumatic event causes a kind of interruption and emotional shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Ibrahimefendic, I've asked you to come to assist the Trial Chamber in assessing the impact on the surviving victims from the events that occurred in Srebrenica in July of 1995. Your organisation, Vive Zene, has treated a number of women and children who were traumatised by the July 1995 events in Srebrenica. Can you tell the Chamber how many women have been treated in your organisation who were traumatised by the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I worked with 60 women in our centre who spent some time at our centre as in-patients, six or seven months, for example, and I carried out a therapeutical programme with about 80 women outside the centre. I think that about 200 -- no, 140 women and 200 children have passed through our centre in total. But I was working with a higher number of people, I had numerous contacts with people from Srebrenica. However, as regards a specific therapy programme, I conducted that kind of programme with the number of people that I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, you mentioned the figure of 200 children. Let me put a different number to you and see if this is a number that might be correct: 300.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I only spoke about the children who were in-house patients as part of the programme, but we worked with another 150 people in Spionica refugee centre, then another 210 in the refugee centre of Nihatovici, and also we worked with children who were part of the programme at our centre. In total, about 300 children were from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the traumatised women and children that your centre has been treating and has been involved with over the years, is that a small percentage of the Srebrenica survivor community that has been traumatised?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a small percentage, indeed, compared to the number of victims in Srebrenica. However, if you bear in mind the fact that there are other organisations in the area of Tuzla and that severe cases are hospitalised, then one can conclude that we did a lot of work for a small number of people. However, bearing in mind the overall situation, the result is, more or less, satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do you have contact in the Tuzla community with other health care providers?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, with other organisations and with a number of other projects that have been applied to the women in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indeed, the number of women who are being assisted by the other health care providers is significantly higher than the numbers that you have mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as I say, what I'd like to do is focus your attention on the impact that the events in July of 1995 had on the women and the children survivors from Srebrenica, and I'd like to get your assessment, if I can. In a global sense, in a macro sense, the level of trauma that you observed the women and the children survivors from Srebrenica suffered in July of 1995 and shortly thereafter, is there a way to inform the Judges as to the degree or the level of trauma suffered by that victim community?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: In my contact with the victims from Srebrenica, women and children, we used various questionnaires in order to assess their psychological condition. We had a number of conversations with them, and on the basis of such conversations, it was possible for us to come up with an assessment as regards the level of trauma. However, we wanted to measure it with certain psychotherapeutical instruments in order to establish the level of trauma in their cases. That level was exceptionally high, and the symptoms that they presented were at a very, very high level of trauma, because the events relating to the month of July 1995 were, globally speaking, events that involved a very large group of women and children and also other survivors, such as elderly people, for example, who all happened to be at one place together, and they experienced that suffering together. For all of them, it was a sudden event, unforeseeable, of course, and it is true that they may have felt a certain safety, security, at one point, but trauma occurs in a sudden manner and it has vast consequences. This all took place in an atmosphere which was beyond their control; there was nothing that they could have done. They were completely helpless. So in such a situation, in Potocari, for example, after this terrible situation in Potocari, when people arrived in Tuzla, the stories that they told were very painful, hard, human stories and very touching. Many women at that point in time simply lost control over their feelings, over their behaviour. The children as well were beyond themselves. Everybody kept asking themselves what was happening and why it was happening. However, the most serious problem was the fact that women and men had been separated. Part of the menfolk had parted with the women and had gone through the woods. One part of the male population stayed with them in Potocari; however, they were separated again in Potocari. Even boys were separated from women in Potocari, and they were wondering what would happen with young boys over the age of ten, for example. So they experienced a large amount of stress immediately after those events and the level of trauma was, indeed, very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. Tell us now, five years have passed since those tragic events, can you comment on the level of trauma that exists today in the Srebrenica survivor community?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Trauma is not forgotten, not because people don't want to forget it. It is stored in the mind and it is remembered, because during such terrible, traumatic moments, all our feelings, everything they feel, they think, they smell, they touch, it is a kind of supermemory which lasts very long, so that those memories are still alive. They have their weight and they have their totality. Among the women we worked with, and we use the sample of women with more serious psychological problems, their memories are still vivid. They still have images of what happened. These are so-called flashbacks. Suddenly, these pictures appear, excerpts from the experience they lived through. In the course of their normal activities, walking around town or somewhere else, they come across something that reminds them and this provokes the flashback. Many of those women still suffer from terrible nightmares, feelings of fear, and other symptoms: irritation, nervousness, aggressiveness, a loss of concentration, irritability. Many avoid talking about those events because they are so painful. These are also symptoms of avoidance. In contact with the victim, we can easily recognise the dominant symptoms depending on the personality, its structure, its mental functions, the way the personality reacts. But if this symptom of avoiding remembering dominates, they become depressive, apathetic, passive. They lose joie de vivre. They don't have the need to communicate with other people. They become isolated and they suffer. It is very difficult to reach out to them. Sometimes they don't want your assistance. They simply say, "I want to die. If they have killed our men, why should I live?" They don't have the strength to face up to their living problems. They lack the willpower; they lack motivation for activity. They see the future in dark colours. They cannot imagine what can happen in a year's time. They feel persecuted because they're living in very difficult conditions. So that five years after the event, I can say that their psychological condition is still extremely grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, you've seen and you have treated, your centre has treated, war trauma victims from other events from other parts of Bosnia, and you've treated as part of your patient group the women from the events in Srebrenica. Are there differences in the trauma characteristics between the women from Srebrenica and traumatised war victims from elsewhere outside of Srebrenica? If there are, can you tell the Judges what those differences might be?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Working with the victims of Srebrenica, I have noticed certain differences and within our team we discussed them. We all agreed that the victims of Srebrenica have something that we have described as the Srebrenica syndrome. They suffer in a special way. They have problems that make them different, especially as of July 1995, because this is a vast number of persons who were in the same place at the same time, and they went through common suffering and they have common shared experiences. On the other hand, at that time the greatest and most stressful traumatic event for them was the disappearance of a large number of men; heads of families, fathers, brothers, uncles, and so on. So that every woman had losses. All the women I worked with had lost two, three, four, five, six persons. A women I worked with, 56 male members of her immediate and broader family went missing in a single day. So the search for the missing, what happened to them? Were they killed? If they were killed, were they tortured? How were they killed? Were they wounded? Were they hungry, thirsty? Where their bones are, the digging up of graves, identification of victims. All these are additionally stressful events, additional traumas that traumatise them on a daily basis. The fact that they do not know the truth -- even the worst truth, would be better for them than this uncertainty, this constant, perpetual uncertainty as to what happened to their loved ones, because they keep waiting, they're waiting for something. They cannot begin life, they cannot face up with the reality of the death of a missing person. They only remember the moment they bade farewell, the moment when they had agreed to meet in a spot that would be safe. And this is still something that still guides them in their thoughts. This is exhausting, discouraging. They think that life has no value. They even become emotionally lacking. And then, of course, there are the children, so the problems are of a much broader scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you believe that, based on your observations, that it will take longer for the Srebrenica women victims to recover, if at all, from the traumas that they experienced, as opposed to other war trauma victims that aren't from the Srebrenica community?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I believe so. I think it will take longer for them to recover, but I'm also certain that some of them will never recover. They will never be able to accept these traumatic experiences, wartime traumas, as a part of their life and to move on, to fit them into their life and to move forward and to continue living. Some of them will remain at the level of waiting and uncertainty till the end of their days. If we were to compare them with victims from other areas of Eastern Bosnia, I should like to point out that the reality of death, no matter how painful and terrible, is far better than thinking about what happened. And women who have received from the International Red Cross certificates that their husbands have been found, at first they had regression in their recovery, namely, they were retraumatised. They again had emotional reactions; they again went through shock and disbelief. But after a certain period of time, they started to recover and they tried to accept the reality of death, to take control over their lives, and to start thinking about the future. For example, a woman asked me, "Tell me, what category do I belong to? I am not divorced. I am not a widow. My husband is missing. Who am I?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Ibrahimefendic, let me focus your attention now on children survivors of Srebrenica, and I'd like you to assist the Trial Chamber in this respect: Can you inform the Trial Chamber of the level of trauma on these child victims, both in 1995, July of 1995 that you observed, and again, that you continue to observe today?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The children witnessed all these events. Many older children witnessed the separation of their brothers and fathers from them. Together with their mothers, they spent time in extremely adverse conditions in Potocari, one, two, or three days, depending. There were small babies of three, four, five, six days old. I worked with close to ten woman who had only just delivered their babies and who reached Potocari with those small babies, and they managed, and they survived, both they and their babies, and they reached Tuzla. Then there were also other children of different ages. And if we take into account the fact that children were in the development stage, then the traumatic effect of those events of 1995 differed. The pre-school-age children demonstrated different symptoms: bouts of crying, excessive attachment to their mothers. They had problems with their appetite, sleeping problems, feeling of fear, because they had watched all that. They were with their mothers, and they followed the reactions of those mothers. School-age children had generalised fear of people, of sounds, persons. They did not want to go to school. They had learning problems, low concentration. They had also these flashbacks. They didn't have anyone to share them with because all of them were suffused with these memories. So they had these terrible nightmares. They would get up at night. Many wet their beds, which had no medical reasons, but they were provoked by psychological reasons. Older children, adolescents, those who managed to survive, both boys and girls, had very high oscillations in their moods and behaviour. Adolescence is a period when they should start out on their own, separated from their parents, but the adult world has undermined their beliefs, their values. The world had suddenly become an insecure place, a place where they cannot feel safe, to which they do not belong. They don't know who they belong to, who they are, even. So their behaviour mostly varied from aggressiveness to withdrawal, isolation -- isolation, lack of activity, spending time at home watching TV or reading. Anyway, keeping to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you notice in July of 1995, then, a high level of trauma amongst these children?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And today, how can you characterise the level of trauma in these children? This is five years after the events that occurred in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Though five years have passed since the events in Srebrenica, I myself am surprised at times, working with children or talking to them, that the images of those events or of fathers, some children had never even seen or remembered, they can't remember them, they were too small, but they still talk about them. In December last year, that is, seven months ago, a boy drew the Udrc Mountain, and he said, "I want to buy myself a helicopter and go there. That is where my father is, and I want to bring him back"; or a little girl of seven who drew her father who is alive and who is still to come back; or an adolescent who told the story that he witnessed the killing of his father. He was extremely withdrawn, though he was involved in a sports programme, but he joined a group that I was working with, the aim of which was social skills and communication skills. But at one point, he started recounting things that had happened five years ago, and all this was accompanied by very turbulent emotional reactions, and he cried like a baby. He is now 17, but he remembered every detail. There are other examples showing that children still talk about what happened because adults are living together in these communities, they have shared experiences. They often talk about them amongst themselves, and these subjects are very much present among the children's thoughts. They sometimes feel they have secrets. They feel guilty because of their reactions. People are exhausted. The women are exhausted talking about what happened, and then they start avoiding it. It's like a conspiracy of silence, which is extremely traumatic in itself. Events cannot be forgotten. They have to be elaborated, analysed, brought out into the open. Some meaning has to be given to them. In a way, they have to put those events in order in their own minds. They have to say such and such a thing happened. I would say that a victim has been treated when she's able to say, "I am a woman of Srebrenica, I have survived, and I want to continue living." But there isn't a woman you can come across who can say that without starting to cry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you have obviously been involved in the treatment of many, many children from Srebrenica. Could you give us an example of one of those children, perhaps, who witnessed the separation of his or her father, and what effects that observation has had through the present day on that child and the child's development.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: There are several examples. For instance, a woman said that together with her husband, she had stayed in Potocari. He was working in the secondary school. He was an educated man, and he believed that nothing would happen to him. And they thought that if he carried the child and -- towards the bus, they would let him on the bus. However, when he got close to the bus, the child was snatched away from him, thrown aside, and he was taken to the other side. It was very crowded. The woman didn't know what to do. Another woman picked up that child, and during the trip to Tisca, to Kladanj, actually, she didn't even know whether her child was in the bus or not. She fainted several times in the bus, and only when they reached Kladanj did a young woman who had picked up her child give it to her. The child is so devoted to his mother that he won't let her out of his sight for a minute. He has to start going to school. She's extremely worried about him because if he starts going to school, they will have to be separated, and he's still extremely attached to her, which is not quite appropriate for his age. There's another example, if I may, of a young boy of ten. He was rather plump and short in size, and then a soldier put his finger on his forehead and asked, "How old are you?" and his mother said "eight"; and he said, "If you had ten, you certainly wouldn't get into the bus." Today he's a frightened child. He is afraid of going anywhere away from the house. Somebody always has to take him with him. He's afraid of various sounds, of people. He is afraid to take a bus alone, to go into a crowd alone. He's always afraid that something might happen to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment on any differences that you have observed between the traumatised children from the Srebrenica victim community and traumatised children from outside of the community, children who were traumatised by events not related to Srebrenica? Are there differences?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: There are differences and they're quite evident. But one of the main reasons, in my opinion, is that children from other areas who were also swept up by the war have preserved their security, and within their family there are male members. So they look for role models among members of the family, among the men of the family; whereas the children of Srebrenica do not have any models they can identify with, especially the boys, and this is one of the main reasons. Another is that the suffering involved a large number of people, as I have already said, in a single day, so that in a very short period of time, a large number of women and children were exposed to a terrible, traumatic event. A third point I would like to make is: The most stressful of all this is the human factor. It wasn't a natural disaster that involved the loss of such a large number of people in such a short time, which makes it even more traumatic. "Why did they do this to us? Did they have to? Why didn't they let our men live? Why? Why? Why?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment on the impact that the Srebrenica events had on these children and how it has affected their social development?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Becoming a refugee, and that in itself is a stressful, traumatic event, has changed the environment they are in. They have reached a new environment. New relationships have to be established, new friends found to feel wanted, to feel more secure. But being encumbered by such traumatic memories, together with the problems of refugee status, made it very difficult. Not only the children, but other members of the family were simply unable to establish any kind of social relationships. They didn't even want to. Social relationships were broken off. There were behavioural problems. They could not communicate either verbally or in other ways. They failed to help one another. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Simply, their entire behavioural patterns changed even in relation to the closest members of their own families. Mothers and children very often have problems of social relationships amongst themselves. There is no direct or transparent communication. Mothers protect children; particularly boys are overprotected. If they are older, they assume the role of adults and they join the adult world too early. For example, one child says, "My father said, 'You are ten, and if your mother falls ill, you will take care of her.'" So he assumes responsibilities, the role of an adult person. The mothers don't want to confide in their children. With the women we worked with in Vive Zene, we tried to improve those relationships so as to encourage them to share their feelings, because this is something that can lead them forward towards recovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. I appreciate your coming here. It's now my colleagues' from the Defence opportunity to ask you questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, we do not have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. I think we should perhaps have a short break before our questions, because I think we do have a few questions to ask, in order not to rush things. Let us have a 20-minute break, and then we'll come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In your very knowledgable display of the situation of the women and children in Bosnia, you pointed out that what you called the Srebrenica trauma syndrome was different from other syndromes which happened in the area during the same period and which perhaps happened in other parts of the world, and you mentioned very different aspects of this trauma. I won't mention what you said. But don't you think this happened also in other areas of Bosnia, where there were victims, not exactly in the Muslim area, but in the Serb area and in the Croat area? What differentiated them, in your opinion, since you have a very lively experience of what happened? What makes this syndrome very special?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Ever since the beginning of the war, Srebrenica was a protected area, and many other people in other parts in Bosnia, looking at a geographical map, would see a very small circle, small area, which was isolated from other parts in Bosnia. There was always a fear from those who lived in Tuzla, and also from women who arrived in Srebrenica in 1993, with whom I also worked in 1994 and 1995, that is, until the fall of Srebrenica, they lived in Tuzla together with their children, their men had stayed in Srebrenica, and they had contact with them through radio communications or through mail via the International Red Cross. So during that period of time they were encouraging themselves to stick it all out, and at that time there were not so many families, such families living in Tuzla. However, there was a number of families that were separated. Men were in Srebrenica, and women and children had come to Tuzla from Srebrenica in 1993. The life in Srebrenica in 1992, 1993, and 1994 was very hard. Women had many fears about their husbands. They didn't know what would happen to them. And that fear kept mounting. They kept oscillating between hope and disappointment, despair. And they asked themselves numerous questions, but they didn't know any answers to their questions. They kept telling themselves, "Well, after all, it's a protected area. Somebody will surely do something," and people were trying to find the solution for Srebrenica. So in the end of June, news was reaching Tuzla from Srebrenica, very bad news. Part of the area had already fallen, including those under the control of the Dutch Battalion. For example, when the observation post fell at Zeleni Jadar, women were still telling themselves, "Well, after all, it's not very far from Srebrenica. The town of Srebrenica itself will be protected and will not fall." But then the fall occurred. And thousands of men abandoned the area of Srebrenica, and they went through the woods and mountains into the unknown in their attempt to reach Tuzla. And as they were parting, they agreed that they would meet there in Tuzla. And while they were in Potocari, women were told that they would be taken care of, and that they would be transported in Tuzla, and that they would meet with their husbands in Tuzla. And during that trip, for instance, in Kravica, many women actually saw captured men. One of the women recognised her husband on one of the trucks. And women were even being used, they would be taken off the truck and forced to call out their husbands from woods and tell them to surrender; one of the women called her husband in that way. And they were hoping that an institution such as the International Red Cross would be able to protect them. They had very high hopes for the lists of people made in Potocari. A number of people were registered on those lists, and they were hoping that they would come. They thought that they would spend some time captured in camps. Such lists contained, for example, 230 names, so they thought that perhaps they would spend some time in camps which have their own regulations, and they hoped that the certain regulations and rules of war would be honoured, and they hoped that they -- that their men would come back. And that is why -- that is the main difference. I think these women have a very profound sense of guilt because they believed that they could have left in 1992, that they could have stayed with them in 1993, for example; and those women who stayed on until 1995, they also think that they could have done something, that they could have foreseen what would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Are you informed about the condition of other women? Are you informed about the condition of other women in other parts of Bosnia where they don't suffer from the same trauma? You mentioned that for Srebrenica it was because there was a very large number in one day. In other parts, you think women are in a better condition, as you said?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. They were not in a better condition, but they could somehow manage their life and they accepted what had happened to them after they were made to leave their homes. Some of the women have husbands who were killed, and they have, in the meantime, managed to accept that fact, and they are more or less able to go on with their lives. But there isn't a single family in Zvornik, for example, that hasn't 20 male members of its family missing. And when you think of the families from Srebrenica, for example, most of the male members from the family are missing. And even though a woman may have, I don't know, five daughters, she feels that she doesn't have anyone because the loss of the male members of their families is especially traumatic for them. There is a woman who lives now with two of her daughters and a small grandchild. She keeps saying, "I don't have anyone." Then I tell her that she has two daughters; she doesn't see it as something valuable. Many women say that they cannot go back to the area of Srebrenica because they don't know who they can go back with. They think that they cannot go there alone. They say, for example, "I cannot build a house alone. I'm afraid. I'm fearful." Out of 170 families with whom I talked in the village of Spionica, in the centre of Spionica, only two persons said that they would perhaps come back within a year; all others said that they were not sure. So this feeling of uncertainty when it comes to the return is also very traumatic for them because they still think that if the men were with them, that things would be much easier for them, that it would be easier for them to make a choice and to go on with their lives. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As far as children are concerned, you mentioned that they are also in a state of great trauma because they have no model to identify with. What is, in your opinion, what's going to be the future of these children? Is the society going to be able to return to normality, or are they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I cannot be that pessimistic because what we are trying to do with them and what other people do with them is we're trying to give them some perspective and to enable them to go on. On the other hand, I am sure that those children will most probably face various problems in their future life, in their future development. This is something that is very difficult to tell. We still don't know. A long-term analysis should be done so that we can perhaps see what the consequences will be. A lady teacher told me her situation. She has a number of children from Srebrenica in her class, and she mentioned the case of a child who told her that his father had disappeared. When she asked the child what his name was, he simply said, "My father disappeared in Srebrenica." That was actually the first sentence that the child said. So that is his identity, the identity of a child whose father had disappeared. Many young people dream of leaving Bosnia, of leaving it all behind. Many adults keep saying that there is no longer any life for them there, any future, and they see future in dark colours. And if you ask them, "Can you picture your daughter or your son in ten years' time," the woman usually replies "No, I cannot." If I ask them, "Can you imagine your children as grown-ups, having their own family," women usually respond negatively. They said, no, that they cannot imagine them in that way because they don't know what is going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They don't even foresee continuing to live normally in a family life and reproducing and so on?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: They want to continue with their life and to educate themselves, but they have various difficulties relating to the adjustment, and it's going to take great effort to achieve the results. They will be focussing their energy to their education and the development of the family life; however, at the same time, they are under a heavy burden. They are unsure as to their identity. They don't know who they are, where they come from. And it is going to take a few years for them to recover because this feeling of life, the joy of life, is no longer there. If they do have some joy of life, then immediately they have a very strong sense of guilt for feeling that. At the same time, they don't feel they are free individuals. A woman once told me, "I'm not a free woman. As long as I am here, unable to come back to my house and see the place where I was born, I am not a free person. As long as my children are not free to visit the area, we are not free persons. Only when that becomes possible, I will be able to think of myself as a human being who does really exist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: With regard to this woman, you mentioned that women who knew that their husbands are dead are in a better position than those who are still waiting. They are not -- are they still expecting their husbands to come back after five years? Is there still -- how is the site living? Are these women still expecting back, or are they getting remarried? And what is the society or the law, what does it allow? Some of them are young; they can start a new life. Do they do that?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: In the past two years and in view of the fact that a lot of mass graves have been excavated, exhumed, and a number of individuals have been identified, so many women now are faced with this problem relating to the identification and the encounter with bodies that have been dug out. So some of the women now have to bury their dead so they have that problem now as to the burial site of their family members. I know only one woman who has remarried. Other women usually do not even think about it, because in most of the cases they are under a heavy influence from the family of their husband, so they cannot actually get married. Another problem is the fact that their husbands are not yet declared dead. They may have been declared missing, but it's them who have to declare them as dead. Only then can they actually remarry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have a background, a very scientific background. Could you put this syndrome, this Srebrenica trauma syndrome, in comparison with other things in your historical studies? If you compare it to the Holocaust, for instance. You mentioned that it's a very specific kind of syndrome. Could you put it in the same category?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: If one takes into account the fact that all detainees in Srebrenica were members of the same ethnic group and that, in a way, that ethnic group was targeted or, as we have had a chance to listen to in the media, that the situation they had found themselves in was a "to be" or "not to be" situation, then in those terms, in those respects, one can perhaps compare the two situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just before I finish. You mentioned that a soldier asked a boy who was going to take the bus, he asked him, "How old are you?" and the boy told him. He told him, "If you are ten --" the boy said, "I am eight." He said, "If you are ten, then you will not get into the bus." Are there examples you know where boys who were ten or over ten were prevented from going with their mothers?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: There are such examples. Women told about how, on the first day, boys who were over 10 or 12 were able to board the buses; however, on the following day, children aged 12 and above were no longer allowed on board. One woman told us about her son who was three years old, and she said that she disguised him as a girl because she was afraid that she would be forced to leave him behind. One woman said that her son's name was Alija, and when they asked her her son's name, she said his name was Danijel because she was afraid to tell them the real name of her son. So when he came to our centre in September 1995, he kept saying, "My name is Danijel. My name is Danijel," and then his mother had to tell him, "No, your name is actually Alija, but I told you that your name was Danijel because I had to." They were fearful even for the very young children. One woman, for example, told us how her son had been taken away and pushed aside, and they asked her, "Well, why would you care about this one child of yours?" This young man suffers from nightmares now. He wakes up in the middle of the night and gets up, and he has certain difficulties, certain problems that necessitate psychotherapy. He was a very withdrawn boy at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. beginning when he came, but he has now severe symptoms that occurred only recently. She came to our centre in 1995 or in 1996 and she came to ask for medical assistance, because there is a medical doctor who is a member of our staff at the centre. She told me how her child was pushed away and how he fell down, and she told us that her son has actually never forgotten that and he's now ten years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You and other people like you who are doing this great humanitarian job, are you trying to -- is there any chance in helping these people to live together again in Bosnia, despite the different ethnic groups? Is there a hope, do you think?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I personally think that that is the only possible choice and a way out and that there is hope. I've had an opportunity to discuss things with people in Srebrenica, people who lived there, and as a person working with traumatised people, I felt that women in Srebrenica who live there today, women of Serbian nationality, are also traumatised. I think that it is very important to speak out, to talk about what has happened. Things happened and they happened at a certain period of time. It is very important for this aggressive impulse to be dealt with, to open it up. Because on the basis of my knowledge about the so-called conspiracy of silence about what has happened, I think that the life amongst us - this is my idea of Bosnia because I have problems saying that Bosnia is a divided country because I spent years living with people from other ethnic backgrounds, and with my friends, I still have contact with all of my friends - I think it is very important that we discuss openly things that happened. Many children are traumatised, and I'm sure that children living today in Srebrenica are very traumatised and need help. I do believe that we should all start a grieving process. We have suffered too many losses, and I believe that this is the only path for us: that we start talking and discussing things openly, that we talk about what has happened. An 80-year-old man who lives in one of the centres said that sometimes individuals are borne on to a group of people who subsequently destroy that group of people, but that on the other hand, there are individuals who raise them again. He said that he needed a certain amount of freedom to pick up his tent, to pitch it up somewhere in Srebrenica, and that that would be enough to restore his sense of freedom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Among the 140 women from Srebrenica and the several hundred children that you have had contact with or treated, are there any success stories? I mean, are there any of those women or those children that, with the help that your centre has been able to provide, appear to have surmounted the obstacles and are on their way to a relatively healthy and normal life? If so, how small a percentage is that of the group that you know?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: At the end of therapy, we had some very significant improvements in terms of the reduction of symptoms and the improved functioning of those women and children. Changes were established in the way of thought, in the expression of feelings, in their behaviour, in their communication with other people, in establishing links with members of their family, with society. But later on there were cases of regression, of the reemergence of those symptoms, so that their condition oscillates. Some women are well on the way to recovery but this is a long-lasting process. If you take into account the context within which they are living now, it is very difficult to talk about a progressive evolution of therapy, a therapy leading to recovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Are you optimistic about the majority of these women and children or only hopeful that some segment will move on to a pretty normal life?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I feel optimistic about their recovery. I want to be an optimist. I want to give them strength; I want to help them to discover their resources, their healthy instincts, so that they can move forward. I keep trying to find what is still sound in their personality so that this might give an impulse for their life in the future, to give meaning to that life. The husband has disappeared, such and such a thing has happened, what can I do now? How can I move on? Where should I start from? I try to make those memories less painful, those images less terrible, so that they should accept them and integrate them into their daily lives, but that is very difficult for the moment. My attitude is an optimistic one, and that is how I behave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The problems that these women have, and their feelings both immediately and now after five years, which you described so eloquently for us, do those feelings make it very difficult, if not impossible, for them to try to continue a community kind of life? In other words, when they are in these centres, et cetera, are they able to reestablish their old customs, their old religious life, a community life of any sort, or are these deep feelings that you've described which interfere with the way the family operates, the relationship with their children, does that also interfere with their ability to reestablish the community kind of connections that they may have had in their former village?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The family was a very strong factor in the villages and family ties were very close. They all sought to preserve those ties because this is precious to them, this is their treasure. By redeveloping those family ties and establishing broader ties with the community, they are trying to establish a future. But here, too, there are ups and downs. For a moment, one may think that things are moving forward, and then already the next minute, this comes to a standstill. Some things that are extremely important for planning for the future have to be addressed; for example, this problem of persecution, the problem of being a refugee. Life as a refugee is extremely distressful. Women do not have any privacy; they don't have any amenities; they live in a single room with several members of the family, and all this has a depressing effect. They all have hopes of returning, of changes, of something else happening. Their original habits and cultural habits that they had in their villages, they're trying to transplant them into the community that they're living in. But very often they suffer from guilt: "I am not allowed to feel any happiness or joy," and this has a particularly detrimental affect on the children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question. You talked some about the differences in the kinds of feelings that were evoked by the women who went through the Srebrenica evacuation as perhaps opposed to other women who suffered from other kinds of injuries in the Bosnian conflict. We've been acquainted with some of those other injuries. Do you think there is a difference, part of the guilt syndrome, that comes from the fact that in some of these other cases, the women themselves have suffered? They've either been in camps or they may have suffered sexual abuse or rape along with the injuries that were inflicted on the men, whereas in this case, the women were taken down one path, sent off to Tuzla, and then the men, as it were, were the object of all of the abuse and of eventual execution? So that there's kind of what we call the Holocaust syndrome. "Why was I allowed to survive when someone else wasn't?" Do you think that's part of the uniqueness of the Srebrenica syndrome?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The feeling of guilt is extremely pronounced among all the women. "I am guilty for not envisaging certain things. I'm guilty for not going together with my husband. I am guilty for not being able to save my child because they took my child, which means I did not fulfil my principal role as a woman. I'm guilty because I can't find my way around alone. I'm guilty if the children have learning difficulties. I'm guilty if they don't get an education." So that this range in the feelings of guilt is a very broad one. "I am also guilty if I were to get married; I would have a very strong feeling of guilt. Maybe I mustn't get married, either. I mustn't even think about another man."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mrs. Ibrahimefendic -- I don't know whether I pronounced your name properly -- I think that we have here a very broad spectrum of questions regarding all the consequences, but I shall try to ask you for a few points of clarification. You spoke about the fact that this was sudden, that they were taken by surprise, that this is a factor, and that this is part of the specificity of the Srebrenica syndrome. The fact that this was a protected area, a safe area, can this also be part of the characteristics of the Srebrenica syndrome; and, furthermore, is this syndrome of guilt, should it be shared by the International Community because it was a protected area?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: If we take into consideration the stories of the women and their explanations for the Srebrenica tragedy, they do put a lot of blame onto the world. "Why didn't they help us? Why did they let us go? Why did they declare us to be a safe area? Why did they let us live for five years in -- for three years in a camp?" That is what women said, where we managed to survive, where we got some food and supplies irregular -- on an irregular basis, where we managed to adjust to that way of life. We Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. started to till the land. We managed somehow to survive, not to starve to death. And one woman said, and several of them, in fact, as far as I can remember, "We had only just started to enjoy life." That is what she said. There were fewer shells. There were no more casualties, because in 1993 they had a large tragedy. 75 people were killed at the stadium in Srebrenica when a shell fell, and Srebrenica was packed full of people. After that, there were no more shells. They would come only sporadically, and then suddenly this happened. We had started to feel safe. We had sort of relaxed. Some women in 1994 got married. I worked with several women who got married in 1994. Life was going on, the kind of life they could give themselves, and then this came as a surprise. It was sudden. Suddenly, they could no longer rely on being safe in a safe area. They were suddenly at risk, and they were slowly approaching Srebrenica town itself. So for them, this was a factor of surprise. They said that in June they might have intimated something, but they didn't believe that it would happen, and until the very last moment they believed that somebody would come to their assistance. All the women said, "Two or three planes flew over, and we were happy. We thought here is help, but nothing happened." And they sought help in the UNPROFOR base. That was the only safe place at the time where they thought they would be protected and that they would be given assistance there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also spoke about the stories of great suffering. You also mentioned that you used various techniques like psychodrama and Gestalt therapy. If we accept these methods of psychotherapy as being most appropriate to facilitate expression, what did you observe in the roles played, in the way people expressed themselves? What are the areas of communication among various members participating in these therapies? Which are the most impressive results in terms of communication achieved by the application of these therapeutic methods?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Applying these techniques and methods, the most significant was evoking the last encounters with loved ones. These were the most painful points when evoking memories. At the beginning of therapy, it was very hard for women to express themselves verbally. In most cases, they couldn't control their emotions, and it took a great deal of time, several months of participation in these projects, for them to express those feelings. And using these methods and techniques, they had to disassociate themselves, in a sense, from their pain, from their anger, from their sorrow, and from the other emotions, and to relieve themselves of them, to feel free of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under those conditions, is it possible for people to refer -- to recreate those painful moments? Because those were seconds; the very moment of separation, that was a second one might say, a few seconds. Those people, do they manage to recreate through role playing that situation?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I have already said that in very traumatic situations, all the sensors are switched on. Sensory reactions are powerful so that everything you feel, see, smell, touch, is deeply embedded in the memory. And in the course of therapy when a woman reaches that level, she can accompany those events with all the emotional reaction she had at the time she experienced that traumatic event. For example, women might say, "I was thirsty. I still feel the touch of my husband's hand. It was sweaty." She would relive the whole experience of that moment. So these are very successful therapies. When a woman manages to express all this, the next time the emotions are not so painful, the images are not so painful; she's more relaxed, less tense. Of course, using all these methods of relaxation, because when a woman is tense, she's unable to express any feelings. So in my work we applied these methods of relaxation because physical tension is extremely harmful, and when they are physically tense, they cannot express their emotions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can one say that these persons have difficulty in perceiving their surroundings, because this supermemory that you have mentioned was and still is under a kind of mortgage, encumbered by those events.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They think that they differ from other people. "I am different; I am special; I am separate; I have experienced this." And it is very important in the course of therapy for that woman to accept that she is a normal person that is reacting normally to an abnormal situation. The situation was abnormal, and she's a normal person, and her reactions are normal. When she accepts this as being normal, then she starts thinking about herself in a different manner. She learns to accept that she is normal. The situation was abnormal. "It was normal for me to react in this way. It was an unusual experience and out-of-the-ordinary experience." So that it is very important for the woman to learn to recognise the symptoms in her, what is happening, why it is happening, why these reactions occurred in which situations, and for her to be able to accept them. And that is extremely important for recovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already mentioned that the absence of information about the destiny of the men in this case, because we are mostly speaking about women, that the absence of this information about the destiny of their men and the importance of exhumation work and identification of bodies. I think you already mentioned this, but the mourning, if we relate this question to marriage or not marriage, is it impossible to mourn without having this information, because as you said, the absence of information provokes anxiety, anxiety provokes tension, permanent tension leads to depression, and so on. So what is the role which the exhumation and identification of bodies can have to somehow reduce all these problems?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think that the agony must be brought to an end. The truth is cruel, but it is the truth, and women are ready to accept the truth, regardless of what they will be told, because they can no longer vacillate in this despair and uncertainty because this is important for their life in the future. What happened? They must know what happened, and they must be given more detailed information about their loved ones. They must know where they will be able to bury them and to perform the regular rites. Some women have already started those rituals linked to the burial, and they accept the truth that the husband is not there on the occasion of religious holidays, for instance, for Kurban. They slaughter a sheep, linked to the death of her husband. In that way, she's recognising that he is dead, but she wants confirmation. She wants a certificate from someone else because she feels terribly guilty if she is the one to have to declare him dead, and this is very, very important for her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think that it could be useful to overcome these difficulties, at least a little, for you to have included in the Srebrenica syndrome the fact there was a large number of people sharing the same suffering, do you think it must be useful, perhaps, to have a monument or a collective ceremony in observance of the missing people or to pay homage to those missing people, men?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: For the people of Srebrenica, this would be evidence, recognition, for the suffering they have lived through. They want this to be observed in a certain place, a certain time so that it be said that people have lived through this, and they have managed to overcome it and their memories and their traumas. Even though they are victims, they want this to be observed in a way, with some kind of material evidence. Every 11th of the month, the women of Srebrenica in Tuzla rally in public places with lists of missing persons demanding the truth. They want more respect for what they have lived through. Somebody has to pay homage to their pain and their sacrifice, and in a sense they wish to share their sorrow, their disappointment, their destiny, and their future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also mentioned the importance of the development of children and adolescents, though each group has different problems, but the importance of development. If we accept that the development is the result between a line of continuity and another line of change which need to be coordinated, from the cultural point of view, is there something that could be done, bearing in mind that in the end, after all, these people have brutally lost continuity by the sudden and violent events, so from the cultural point of view, could we resume this process of social identification? Is there something that can be done in that direction? Sorry, are you doing something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: In our work, we are working in several directions, and we are seeking to cover all our clients by treatment and to help them function in all spheres: emotional, social, behavioural. We seek to develop a social net, a system of social support within which they will feel safe and accepted. However, the problem with young people and children is that they are trying to deny what has happened, trying to forget it, to put it aside. They do not wish -- they cannot face up to it, they cannot accept that that is a part of their life and to live with the truth of it. The problem of denial is present among young people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't, of course, wish to establish any kind of a programme here, but perhaps a revision of history could help to reformulate, review, and learn. Perhaps from the point of view of the plan of education or a revision of history, the teaching of history, do you think that something should be done, any changes should be made? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think that would be the proper solution, to revise what has happened, to perhaps establish the historical background for everything that happened. An explanation needs to be given as to what happened. Children cannot understand what it is that happened; even adults, many adults don't understand. I know that whenever I had group therapy and tried to give an historical explanation for what happened, that the rational acceptance of what happened was far more successful and contributed to the recovery of those women. It is very important for them to receive the proper information and to rationalise the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small point of clarification. You mentioned that children have problems and symptoms of -- development symptoms. Are things moving forward a little, after all?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: You mean in a positive direction? I'm afraid I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there's a problem of translation. You said that children have many neurotic -- neurosis symptoms -- sorry, bed-wetting. After they had outgrown these problems, are things going further? Do they even relieve themselves in bed, have a bowel movement in bed? Does that happen sometimes?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: People who receive therapeutic assistance are very happy, but unfortunately we can't provide everyone with this treatment. We have very good results with the reduction of bed-wetting in children who, because of trauma, have this problem. However, we can't cover a large number of children. It is a fact that some women do not want any assistance. They're isolated, they're passive, and they don't accept any assistance. They reject it. They say, "No one can help me. My life is what it is and I don't want to change anything." But we have some very positive results among children treated in our centre. Great improvements were achieved in their behaviour. If they were aggressive or withdrawn, if they had this problem of bed-wetting or if they had terrible dreams or if they were very bad at school or if they lacked motivation, by various methods, techniques, and activities, we worked with them in groups and individually and we have some very good results. But unfortunately all children are not covered by such treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is said that the first step towards dealing with a problem is to start talking about it; that is a general principle. But I think that here that principle does not hold true. Does this principle, in your opinion, apply to this situation, or are there other requirements, other steps to be taken to address this problem? Because it is not a situation of normal treatment, but other techniques need to be applied, other resources and other concerns taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: To deal with these problems, it is important to have a multifold approach. One is therapy. To deal with a problem, it is true that one has to start to talk about it. But there are many other problems that need to be resolved in the community: social problems, political problems, economic problems, for an improvement to be achieved. It is a fact that the very principle that someone starts talking about a problem, starts verbalising his needs and wishes, is already the first step indicating that he is seeking assistance. That is very important, for people to emerge from their passiveness and to start to fight for themselves, to demonstrate a wish to fight. But there are other aspects too which need to be taken into consideration. Contacts are very important to establish, interpersonal contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, and I quote you: "It is not possible to engage in long-term research." Do you think that in terms of the consequences of several events, and in this particular case we're talking about Srebrenica, can we stop with the results we have achieved or should we really engage in research, applying follow-up methods, so that we can have a more global view of the situation?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think we need to have a global approach as to what has happened because we are acting in a disunited manner, and I think our efforts need to be pooled, and possible follow-up studies should be engaged in to see the changes that will occur. To foresee the future of a child who is dislocated, for whom the world has become an unsafe place, a child that doesn't have a home, who has lost his father, who is living in a refugee centre under very difficult conditions, it is very difficult to foresee his future. A global approach would help us all to feel safer and to know in which direction we should all focus our efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put to you a last question. Of course, there are many questions but we need to finish with this testimony. You are practically involved in these developments; you are familiar with the environment and the surroundings. Could we not come to an absurd situation, that the persons who are dead are happier than those who have survived, or more fortunate, rather?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Those who have survived do not feel happy. They have a large number of problems. Many women say, "Why am I alive when others are dead?" They say that very often. "Why do I have to struggle with all the difficulties that life entails? I just can't deal with them." But I think that those who have survived need to be given a meaning to life. Life does have meaning regardless of what they have lived through. In my practical work, as you have said, I frequently say to the women, "If you don't tell me the story about your son, I don't know him, and therefore if you are gone, no one will ever hear the story about him." So I try to instil in them the feeling that life does have a meaning regardless, that life in itself is burdensome, that in life we do have to encounter many difficulties and changes; that people with no traumatic experiences, experiences involving risk to life, are fortunate but that life is a struggle, and we have to confront all those problems and misfortunes that come our way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You touched upon a point. I think that the whole of humanity, in my opinion, this is a humanitarian cause, and the whole of mankind should be interested, and the International Tribunal, as a part of the community, must pursue the objectives that are yours. You have experience. What do you think should be the role of the Tribunal? Please feel at ease and feel free to tell us what you think. Specifically, in this courtroom, what kind of role should it play, because this is the courtroom that victims come to. And you already have certain indications about that.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The Hague Tribunal, all the victims, all the women with whom I have had a chance to work, has a very great significance for them. They expect that justice will be done. We believed we were members of a civilised society, of a society where good will be compensated for and evil punished. They do trust that the real causes of what happened will be identified and that the people will muster enough courage, including victims, to tell the story of what happened. Those who did it, that they too will be able to speak out so that we all can have a future, so that we all can have a basis for a common life together one day. Great expectations are being placed upon the Tribunal. People expect that justice will be done and that the right decisions will be reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that my colleague Judge Fouad Riad has one more question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. [In English] Ms. Ibrahimefendic, in fact, my question is based on some of the answers you gave to my colleagues, my very eminent Judge colleagues, which touched on a very basic problem, a very basic issue, and this is the planning for the future and the continuation of life for this community, because some communities could not rise up again after destruction in history, some continents even.
