In this community in particular, some of the other experts who spoke here mentioned to us that in this Islamic community, it's a patriarchal society, with all the effects of a patriarchal society. The man is the spine. I will give you an example. One of the ladies who had five daughters said, "These girls don't count. I want a man. I want a boy," or that sort of thing. We know that. Now, with the men who disappeared, how can this society, as my colleague Judge Rodrigues asked you, how can they continue in a changed -- he said, even with a coordinated change? How could they go along this new line without the spine, when this society was revolved around the man? Could they completely change, completely become a very ultramodern society, or is there a chance of this complete change? Will it be like a snowball and the society will disintegrate more and more? Can the women remarry? Can they stand on their feet? Can the boys and the girls resume their lives? Perhaps this is psychological and sociological, and it's your field. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think that there should be a change in the behaviour of those women. The women we worked with, we tried to make them realise that they have to take life in their own hands, that they have to assume responsibility for a number of problems that would normally be taken care of by men, that they have children and consequently have responsibility regarding their children. So there have been certain changes in that regard. Many women would like to go back, for example, to go back and start a new life, because the economic situation is very hard. They have had enough of the refugee life; they feel it has become unbearable. In that view, the role of the woman has changed. I think that it will be very interesting to see in what way the role of the women will change in these patriarchal, Islamic families. This concerns the rural areas to a greater extent, because in towns women have their jobs, their professions, and they are able to live on their own. So we should focus on the necessity for the women to assume responsibility for their own life and to have them become like men in certain aspects of life. In patriarchal families, women who tend to struggle, who are somewhat aggressive in that way, are not valued enough, but life circumstances have changed for them, and many of these women have changed. They have become more spontaneous, more independent, and little by little they are resolving problems which were very difficult at the beginning for them. This concerns, for example, administrative problems, because before they would never go out into the public to various public institutions to take care of the bureaucracy, but this is slowly changing, and they are now involved in that aspect of life as well. The absence of men has already changed them to a certain extent, as has the life of a refugee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You added when you were answering Judge Wald that family is an important factor, very important factor in this rural life, and it's a factor in life for the continuation of life. Can these women, now that the men have disappeared, can they remarry without being looked down upon by society as being not, not in a tradition of faithfulness and so on? Can life be resumed, really, in this area?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think that many women still think about having a man and remarrying, but many women do not have anyone to marry because there are not many men in such an environment, so it is very difficult to discuss these issues with women. Not only in Srebrenica, but elsewhere in Bosnia, many young people left, left the country as early as the beginning of 1992. And later on, during the war many people abandoned, left the country, and they're still doing that. So I've heard people say that Bosnia is the country of women. There are very many women in Bosnia. And in the settlements where they live, there are mostly women and children. There is very few men left who have survived and who are living in these centres. In the Spionica settlement, there are 90 single mothers out of 170 families. I think that there are about 20 married couples, and the rest is the elderly population, over 70, including elderly men. So these are very particular social problems which may lead -- or may, rather, affect the continuation of life in those parts of the world. Certain men have survived, but they have their own families, and they are surrounded by a number of women who don't have husbands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In this very closed environment, did the percentage of birth decrease substantially?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the year 2000, but there was an increase at one point in birth rate in previous years in Tuzla, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How much was the decrease in your opinion in the last years?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to provide a precise answer to your question because Tuzla was the place where many refugees found accommodation, and the town population has become older. There were a number of births in 1996. There was an increase, actually, in births at that time, but a lot of people have moved out, so it's very difficult to give you precise information about that. But perhaps I should give you an example: Out of 1.500 people living in the settlement of Mihatovici in the settlement of Tuzla, last year the pre-school population programme was focussed on 80 children; however, now we have only 22 such children taking part in that programme. But in 1996, for example, not all children could be admitted into the pre-school programme of education, but things have changed and there has been a decrease, and we would actually be able to admit many more children in such programmes than before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us finish with a question. How many generations do you think it will take for the life to return to normal?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour, to answer your question by an example. A Jewish psychotherapist living in the States once took part in a programme here, and I had an opportunity to be present at four of such sessions in Bosnia. The objective of those sessions was for us to speak out, and her idea was to have a group of professionals from the federation and from the Serbian entity of the country and to have us start talking about what happened together. I must say that I was looking forward to taking part in that work, and that that was -- and that the initial contact with our colleagues from the Serbian entity was rather disappointing. At least, I was disappointed in a way. However, the following three encounters yielded certain results. They were actually quite successful, and we realised that we had certain ideas in common, that we were able to think about what has happened and to accept what we have all been through together. We were able to share memories and to start the grieving, the mourning process and the reconciliation process, and we were beginning to be able to accept that as part of our lives. However, it is very difficult for me to tell you how many generations it will take for us to be able to live a normal life, as you put it. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Ibrahimefendic, we have come to the end of your testimony, and I think that we have managed to reach an answer to the questions that was posed by Shakespeare, "To be or not to be," as you put it while you were discussing the possibility of comparing that tragedy to the Holocaust. So I think that we have realised that the question that has -- that we all have to ask ourselves is what it means to be a human being. We would like to wish you a lot of success in your work. It is indeed a very important work and an enormous work. And we also hope that you will be able to cooperate with your Serbian or Croat colleagues in order for all of you to be able to restore a multi-ethnic community where the dignity of the individual will be one of the fundamental values. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Thank you very much, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, for coming here. We wish you a lot of success in your future work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we will adjourn for the day, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will adjourn after the conclusion of testimony of this witness, but I would like to tender for purposes of this phase of our case certain affidavits, and then I have nothing further for today. So with the Court's permission, pursuant to Rule 94 ter, we filed a number of affidavits on July the 20th, and we have shared these affidavits with our colleagues. They have no objection to our presenting these affidavits. I would add, however, and emphasise that these affidavits, first, are a small sample of views of people who were in the victim community in Srebrenica. Many of these affidavits contain facts, and we are asking the Trial Chamber to consider the facts contained in each of these affidavits only on the issue of victim impact and not to consider the facts as additional evidence or for any other purpose. So if I could, Mr. President, we would tender affidavits that are Exhibits 714 through 721, and then further affidavits 723 through 733. These affidavits contain both an affidavit sworn in accordance with the law of the State of Bosnia, and they also contain a supporting statement of the affiant that was taken by the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us hear the Defence on this. Mr. Visnjic, do you have any objections or comments to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the documents mentioned by the Prosecutor, that is, the exhibits under the numbers stated, were received by the Defence a while ago. We managed to review them. It is true that they contain certain facts which would be subject to an examination of witnesses, direct examination of witnesses. However, I should agree with Mr. Harmon when he said that the probative value of this evidence should be restricted or, rather, limited to the consequences of the events that the victims have suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I should like the Chamber to note this objection of the Defence which is actually part of an attitude that we share with the Prosecution in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the exhibits that have been tendered will be admitted into evidence, and the facts contained therein should be taken into account only to the extent they relate to the consequences suffered by the victims. The documents are therefore admitted under that caveat. Mr. Harmon, shall we call it a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we should. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We will therefore adjourn until tomorrow, 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday the 28th day of July, 2000, at 09.30 a.m.
